messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 42
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Farmer
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event, Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark, Certain Songs: Certain songs
  Maladaptive Strategies: Delay Sleep: stay up until very late, Avoid People: avoid other people, Avoid Sleep: Going to sleep or lying in the dark
  Memory: Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Sokha is a 42-year-old Cambodian American farmer who came to treatment months after his young son survived a life-threatening illness that had unfolded over several nights with terrifying speed. He described the worst part not as a single medical fact but as a set of images that never seemed to leave him: his boy’s small chest pulling hard for air, the bluish color around his lips, the thin wrists and hands that felt too cold when Sokha held them in the emergency room. During those nights he had sat awake under harsh hospital lights, listening to monitors and to the same soft songs that drifted from a nurse’s station radio and later from his own phone when relatives called to check in. Darkness had become fused with helpless waiting. Waking in the night now carried him straight back to those hours when he believed his son might die before morning.

After his son recovered, Sokha expected the fear to settle. Instead, pieces of the experience began returning abruptly. If he caught sight of a child’s ribs while helping his family in the fields, or noticed a hand, a mouth, a chest moving under a shirt, he could feel his body jolt as though he were back beside the hospital bed. At night, if he woke in the dark before dawn, the memory did not feel like remembering. It felt present, immediate, as if he were once again leaning over his son and checking whether he was still breathing. Certain songs were especially potent. A melody playing from a truck radio at the farm stand or from a neighbor’s phone could bring a sudden fragment of the hospital into his mind and then leave him shaken, trying to orient himself to where he actually was.

Because these moments came on so forcefully, Sokha began organizing his life around not being caught by them. He stayed up very late most nights, often sitting with the television on or scrolling on his phone until exhaustion forced him to sleep, because lying down in the dark felt too close to those nights of waiting. He also found reasons to keep away from people. At the farm, he took solitary tasks when he could and avoided lingering conversations, especially with other families, because he feared being trapped while one of those flashes hit him. The songs and the dark had taught him that ordinary moments could turn suddenly unbearable, and he came to believe that distance and wakefulness were the only ways to stay ahead of it.

Yet the less he slept and the more he narrowed his days, the more brittle everything became. When he was overtired from delaying sleep, dawn chores in the fields felt unreal and exposed. In that fog, the sight of an arm reaching across a produce crate or a child being carried near the roadside stand could catch his eye with unusual force, and nighttime itself seemed to start earlier in his mind, long before sunset. Avoiding people also made the triggers feel larger. Without conversation or distraction, small details stood out too sharply: a song in the distance, the outline of a throat swallowing, a hand resting limp in someone’s lap. His efforts to prevent the fear had the effect of making the world feel more crowded with reminders.

The memories themselves pushed him further into those habits. When sudden pieces broke through, they did not arrive as a story with a beginning and end. He would get only his son’s lips, or the sight of his chest, or the sense of standing in a dark room waiting for something terrible to happen. Because the memory felt as if it were happening now rather than long ago, Sokha would resist going to bed that night, certain that sleep meant surrendering to it. Some evenings he remained outside or in the kitchen long after his wife had gone to bed, unwilling to lie in the dark where he expected the hospital to return. He knew this was straining the household; his wife had begun asking why he was never really present with her, and at work he was less available during shared tasks, choosing isolation over the risk of being seen shaken.

Over time, the memories also seemed to teach him what to fear. A flash centered on his son’s mouth or chest made him scan those body parts in other people without meaning to, and once he noticed them, the sense of danger surged again. A fragment tied to waking in darkness made every nighttime awakening feel like the start of another catastrophe. A song that had once accompanied phone calls from worried relatives could turn an ordinary afternoon at the farm into a scene charged with dread. By the time he sought help, Sokha was sleeping only in short stretches and spending more and more of his life bracing against reminders he could not reliably avoid. What finally brought him in was the fear that his son was recovering while he himself was not—that he was becoming a man who could no longer be fully with his family after sunset, and that if he kept living this way, the nights would always belong to the hospital.
